selected.title: November rate rise less likely with inflation data lower than expected
selected.summary: The odds of the Reserve Bank lifting interest rates in November have fallen sharply after the latest consumer price index (CPI) came in lower than expected. News figures from the ABS show show headline inflation jumped to 4 per cent in the year to August.
selected.why: Surprising CPI data significantly alters expectations for upcoming RBA monetary policy decisions.

( ABC News: Sharon Gordon ) In short: Headline inflation jumped to 4 per cent in August, from 3.5 per cent in July, driven by higher housing costs and automotive fuel prices. But underlying inflation remained at 3.6 per cent for the third month in a row. What's next? Some economists think another rate rise is likely, though money markets are predicting there is only a 20pc chance of a November hike. abc.net.au/news/inflation-august-2026-australia-bureau-of-statistics/107210688 Link copied Share Share article The odds of the Reserve Bank lifting interest rates in November have fallen sharply after the latest consumer price index (CPI) came in lower than expected. Annual headline inflation jumped to 4 per cent in August, up from 3.5 per cent in July , according to the Bureau of Statistics (ABS). It was slightly lower than the 4.1 per cent inflation that economists were predicting ahead of the official numbers being released. But trimmed mean inflation, the RBA's preferred measure of underlying inflation, remained steady at 3.6 per cent for the third month in a row. The ABS numbers show that consumer prices are still rising, but at a slower rate than was expected. The news comes a day after the central bank lifted interest rates for the fourth time this year, to their highest level in 15 years , to try to drag inflation down and stop high inflation becoming embedded in Australia's economy. Money markets are now betting the RBA will likely keep rates on hold at its next meeting in early November. The odds of a rate hike fell to around 20 per cent, according to market data from LSEG. reason: Australian timing; RBA policy at inflection point with conflicting signals (headline up, trimmed mean flat, markets vs economists diverge)
angle: The RBA should hold rates now because underlying inflation's stability matters more than headline volatility, and further hikes risk unnecessary damage to employment.
